title: Mishpatim: your enemy's donkey (Exodus 23:4–5)
hookLine: return your enemy's straying ox and help his fallen donkey up
tomorrow: Mishpatim: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:21–23)

lines: THE NEIGHBOR NOBODY GETS ALONG WITH.
cards: Say there's a neighbor nobody on the street gets along with. Maybe he called the city about a fence. Maybe she said something at a meeting that still stings.
People time their trips to the mailbox. Then one morning, out the window, his dog has gotten loose and is trotting toward the highway. Or her car is stuck in the snow, wheels spinning.
Nobody else is around. The Torah, in the middle of laws about honest courts, imagines exactly this moment, in a world of oxen and donkeys.

teach.b: The first law, in the old Jewish translation: "If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray," you must bring it back to him. Not a friend's. Your enemy's.
The second law goes further. You see the donkey of someone who hates you lying under its load, and you may want to walk past. Don't.

teach.h: AZOV AND AZOV: LEAVE, OR UNLOAD.
teach.b: The Hebrew plays on words: you might want to leave him, azov, but you must help, also azov, a twin verb meaning to unload. And the verse says help with him.

teach.h: RASHI: WITH HIM, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Rashi points out: with him. The owner works too; it's a job for both of you, side by side, hands on the same ropes. Notice what the Torah doesn't say.
It doesn't say you have to like him, or that the grudge is wrong. It says the animal is suffering and his loss is still a loss, so act anyway. The Talmud pushes the idea one step further.
Suppose a friend's donkey needs unloading and an enemy's needs loading. Normally the animal in pain comes first.
But here, the Talmud says, help your enemy first, in order to bend your own inclination.
The point isn't only the donkey. It's what happens between two people who have pulled on the same rope in the mud.

how: Jewish law counts returning lost property, hashavat aveidah, and helping unload a fallen animal as commandments, and the Talmud's rule to help an enemy first is taught as training the heart through action.

o: ordinances: laws for courts and daily life
the elders chosen to judge the small cases
a word for the tablets of the covenant

games.q: inside the donkey law — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah says you must like your enemy
it doesn't. it says act anyway: return the ox, help with the donkey.
the Talmud says to help an enemy before a friend, in one case
to bend your own inclination, it says.
you're meant to do all the work while the owner watches
the verse says help with him. Rashi: the owner works too.

games.q: you see the donkey of someone who hates you, lying under its load. no one else is around. what does the Torah say?
o: help him release it, side by side.
games.why: help with him. not because you like him, but because the animal is down and his loss is still a loss.

practice: Think of someone ordinary and irritating, not your worst enemy, and picture them stuck: a flat tire, a dropped box of groceries, a crashed laptop the night before a deadline.
Picture yourself walking over, not liking them, just helping, your hands and theirs on the same problem. If you pray, you can hold them there for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Mishpatim. The ordinances. Today, the law that sends you back with your enemy's ox, and to his fallen donkey, to help with him.

orig.note: Hebrew: donkey. the animal at the center of the law about helping an enemy.

carryVoice: Your line: help your enemy's donkey. A week since Sinai: one heart, eagles' wings, the first word and the last, the details, the stranger. That's day three hundred fifty.
